topic_text: The value of goods and services produced in the UK.
text:
UK gross domestic product (GDP) shows an estimated fall of 0.2% in Quarter 3 (July to Sept) 2022. There was a slowing on the quarter for the services, production and construction industries; likely because of energy price rises affecting household disposable incomes.

It is important to note that data for September 2022 (and a lesser extent the Quarter 3 estimates) are affected by the bank holiday for the State Funeral of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, where some businesses operated differently on this day.

topic_text: How much the production and services industries contribute to economic output.
text:
Monthly production output rose by 0.3% between November and December 2022 and is 1.4% below February 2020; this was the last month of 'normal' trading conditions before the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The monthly increase in output resulted from growth in two of the four production sectors, with electricity and gas rising by 5.2% and water supply and sewerage by 0.7%; this was partially offset by mining and quarrying, which fell by 4.6%.

Output remained below the February 2020 pre-coronavirus pandemic levels in the mining and quarrying (17.2% below) and manufacturing (2.3% below) sectors; in contrast, water supply and sewerage and electricity and gas were above the February 2020 level, at 11.0% and 5.3% respectively.

Monthly services output fell by 0.8% between November and December 2022 and remains 0.7% below February 2020, which was the last month of 'normal' trading conditions prior to the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The Index of Services (IoS) saw falls in 11 of the 14 sectors during December 2022; with human health and social work activities seeing the largest fall, contributing negative 0.25 percentage points to IoS growth (with growth falling by 2.8%).

topic_text: Measures of demand in the economy for output that is produced.
text: Retail sales volumes are estimated to have increased by 0.5% in January 2023, following a fall of 1.2% in December 2022 (revised from a fall of 1.0%); sales volumes were 1.4% below their pre-coronavirus (COVID-19) February 2020 levels.

Business investment in the UK fell by 2.5% in Quarter 3 (July to September) 2022. This figure has been revised down from the provisional estimate of a 0.5% fall.

Whole economy investment (technically known as Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF)), which includes business and public sector investment, grew by 1.1%.

Although this is lower than the provisional estimate of 2.5%, overall investment in this area and the majority of its components remain above pre-coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic levels. In Quarter 3 2022, whole economy investment was 0.2% above its pre-coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic level and 3.7% above Quarter 3 2021.

Positive growth in residential property has been the main factor in whole-economy investment returning to pre-pandemic levels. In Quarter 3 2022, growth in this sector remained positive at 1.0%. Although this revised figure is slower than the provisional estimate of 4.2%, it is 12.4% above pre-pandemic levels.

Whole economy investment in non-residential buildings and structures like roads, bridges and energy-related structures is now 8.3% below its pre-coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic level.

topic_text: Demand and supply of labour in the economy and how much employees earn.
text: The employment rate was estimated at 75.6% for October to December 2022, 0.2 percentage points up on the year and 0.2 percentage points up on the quarter.
The unemployment rate was estimated at 3.7% for October to December 2022, 0.3 percentage points down on the year but 0.1 percentage points up on the quarter.

Average weekly earnings for employees in Great Britain in nominal terms (not adjusted for inflation) increased by 5.9% for total pay (including bonuses) and 6.7% for regular pay (excluding bonuses) in October to December 2022.

topic_text: Changes in prices of goods and services bought by consumers, as well as those bought and sold by producers in the UK.
text:
The Consumer Prices Index including owner occupiers' housing costs (CPIH) 12-month inflation rate was 8.8% in January 2023, down from 9.2% in December 2022.

Consumer price inflation can be influenced by the strength of domestic supply and demand, and changes in the UK prices of imports. The inflation rate also depends on price levels in the preceding year.

Producer output (factory gate) prices rose by 13.5% in the year to January 2023, down from 14.6% in the year to December 2022.

Changes in the output Producer Price Index inflation rate can be influenced by changes in labour and energy costs.

Producer input prices rose by 14.1% in the year to January 2023, down from 16.2% in the year to December 2022.

Input prices are influenced by raw material prices and exchange rate movements so are more changeable over time.

topic_text: UK exports and imports of goods and services and measures of foreign direct investment.
text:
The value of goods imports increased by £1.6 billion (2.9%) in December 2022; after removing the effect of inflation, imports of goods increased by £0.7 billion (1.5%).

Goods imports from EU countries increased by £1.0 billion (3.8%) and imports from non-EU countries rose by £0.5 billion (1.9%).

Gas prices increased sharply in December 2022, contributing to a £2.0 billion increase in the value of gas imports from Norway.

The value of goods exports decreased by £0.8 billion (2.3%) in December 2022, linked to a fall in exports to non-EU countries; after removing the effect of inflation, total exports of goods decreased by £0.1 billion (0.3%).

The total trade in goods and services deficit, excluding precious metals, widened by £2.4 billion to £26.8 billion in Quarter 4 (Oct to Dec) 2022, driven by lower exports of both goods and services.

The trade in goods deficit, excluding precious metals, widened by £1.0 billion to £64.0 billion in Quarter 4 2022, while the trade in services surplus narrowed by £1.4 billion to £37.2 billion.

The total annual trade in goods and services balance, excluding precious metals, widened by £85.3 billion to a deficit of £108.0 billion in 2022 when compared with 2021, driven by a 32.5% increase in import values.

measure: FDI - liabilities (overseas investment into the UK)
text: UK direct investment liabilities were £1,287.6 billion in April to June 2016, up slightly from £1,272.4 billion in the previous quarter. FDI liabilities were following a broadly upward trend in previous years, before falling in January to March 2016.

UK direct investment assets were £1,414.7 billion in April to June 2016, up from £1,349.5 billion in the previous quarter. The value of FDI liabilities has fluctuated over the past two years, although remains broadly similar to levels seen in 2012.
